item.title: First Chapter: 'What Are Journalists For?'
item.description: This book review discusses Jay Rosen's advocacy for public journalism, a movement aiming to transform journalism by prioritizing citizen input and engagement. The review highlights the debate surrounding public journalism, with supporters viewing it as a way to improve political discourse and critics dismissing it as a fad or overreach. The review also notes the movement's waning influence in recent years, despite its impact on some news organizations.

item.title: Some feel media needs to give Kennedys time, space
item.description: An article examining media coverage of the JFK Jr. plane crash and death, discussing whether reporters should give the Kennedy family more privacy during their time of grief. Experts including Jay Rosen from the New York University Graduate School of Journalism are quoted about the media's performance and the balance between public interest and family privacy.

item.title: The moral confusion of the media
item.description: Article discusses moral and ethical challenges facing contemporary media. References Jay Rosen's work for the Nieman Foundation in the context of a discussion about new journalism and media ethics.

item.title: What Are Journalists For?
item.description: Jay Rosen's 1999 book (Yale University Press) on the public-journalism movement. item.title: What Are Journalists For? - Rosen, Professor Jay: 9780300078237 - AbeBooks
item.description: This book recounts the history of the public journalism movement, which emerged after the 1988 presidential election as a response to declining trust in the news media and public disillusionment with politics. Rosen, a key figure in the movement, examines both the theoretical underpinnings and practical applications of public journalism, exploring the question of whether journalists should be passive observers or active participants in public conversation and civic action.

item.title: Good news
item.description: Article discusses the concept of 'good news' or 'solutions journalism' and its challenges in gaining traction in mainstream media. Jay Rosen is identified as a leader of the civic journalism movement and is quoted on the prospects for solutions journalism.

item.title: Caring response, or cynical ploy?
item.description: A media commentary column by Mark Jurkowitz examining a newspaper's response to a school shooting and whether its community-focused coverage represents genuine civic journalism or a cynical marketing ploy. The article discusses public journalism and references Jay Rosen as a 'New York University journalism professor' and authority on the public journalism movement, connecting the newspaper's approach to broader debates about journalism's role in communities.

item.title: Public backs paper's handling of Ore. shootings
item.description: Article discusses public reaction to The Oregonian's coverage of school shootings, including quotes from media experts assessing the paper's approach. Jay Rosen is quoted praising the paper's handling of the coverage.

item.title: Gee! Seinfeld's on a magazine cover
item.description: Maybe that's, human nature being what it is, enough to satisfy the civic impulse that motivates the Rosen and the civic journalism movement.

item.title: Work together for city's future
item.description: An editorial discussing a community forum where Spokesman-Review staff and community members spent time with New York University Professor Jay Rosen discussing how news media can strengthen civic culture. The editorial encourages community cooperation for the city's future.

item.title: Volusia today
item.description: A brief news item about a panel discussion on news media and civic dialogue. Jay Rosen from NYU is identified as a panelist who specializes in public journalism. The event runs from 1-5 p.m. Saturday and 1-4 p.m. Sunday.

item.title: Stetson media forum: News media and the community
item.description: Brief announcement for a Stetson University media forum titled 'News Media and the Community — A Vision Dialogue' to be held at Stetson University. The forum featured nationally known journalists and media experts including New York University professor Jay Rosen, along with Washington Post political columnist David Broder and others, examining the news media's role in shaping community and civic dialogue.

item.title: College students look at local news coverage and see a lot of bias
item.description: An article about college students analyzing local news coverage for bias. The article mentions an upcoming panel discussion featuring Washington Post media writer Howard Kurtz and Jay Rosen, who holds the Chair in Media Ethics and Press Policy at New York University.

item.title: Talking heads
item.description: This article discusses changes in the format and content of news shows, and how they are trying to adapt to maintain relevance. It mentions Jay Rosen in relation to someone trying to find out what people need to know.

item.title: Re-examining Reporting
item.description: This article by David Miles discusses Davis Merritt's views on and involvement in public journalism, including his efforts to revitalize civic life through journalistic practices.

item.title: A newspaper can be a catalyst for community dialogue
item.description: A viewpoint article exploring the role of newspapers in facilitating community dialogue and civic engagement. The article mentions Jay Rosen as an author and professor who writes on the topic of public journalism and newspapers' potential to serve as catalysts for community conversation.

item.title: Book example of how media miss real issues
item.description: Book review discussing 'The Choice' and how media coverage misses real political issues, focusing on consultants rather than substance. Jay Rosen is mentioned as someone who studies media coverage.

item.title: MEDIA from A21 Skepticism is considered a key quality of journalism
item.description: The article discusses the role of skepticism in journalism and how journalists cover newsworthy events.

item.title: 'Choice' pays too little attention to issues
item.description: A review of Bob Woodward's book 'The Choice' discusses the book's focus on campaign strategy rather than issues. Jay Rosen is quoted as a public journalism leader criticizing the book's premise and focus on political consultants.

item.title: Inside again: The choice was ... theirs
item.description: Review of Bob Woodward's book 'The Choice' which covers the 1996 presidential election. The review mentions that the book gives little evidence of the 'public journalism' movement, with Jay Rosen identified as its evangelist.

item.title: Work in progress: Can public journalism save a troubled profession?
item.description: A book review discussing public journalism and its potential to revitalize the troubled journalism profession. The review mentions Jay Rosen, described as a former New York University journalism professor, as a key figure in the public journalism movement.

item.title: Getting the Connections Right: Public Journalism and the Troubles in the Press (Perspectives on the News)
item.description: At the same time, the profession itself is facing economic decline, as well as challenges from new information and communication technologies that threaten to eclipse traditional journalism. What is a journalist to do?Jay Rosen makes the case that journalists can avoid succumbing to these worrisome trends by practicing what is increasingly being called "public journalism." What is needed is a new connection between public and press, one in which the press recognizes its influence in public life and helps citizens to participate, and be fully informed and engaged.

item.title: "Public journalism" - just another way of doing what we've always done
item.description: Article discusses the concept of public journalism and its various forms. Jay Rosen is mentioned as someone who has written extensively about and analyzed public journalism, with reference to reviewing the literature on the subject.

item.title: Newspaper 'public journalism' effort to revitalize public life triggers debate
item.description: An article discussing the public journalism movement and the debate it has sparked within the newspaper industry. The article identifies Jay Rosen as the person who coined the term 'public journalism' and serves as director of the Project on Public Life and the Press at New York University.

item.title: Public Journalism A Case for Public Scholarship
item.description: Jay Rosen argues for "public journalism," a movement reforming the American press. He critiques the existing disconnect between journalism practice and academic theory, advocating for collaborative, participatory approaches that prioritize civic engagement and a deliberative public sphere. Rosen highlights examples of newspapers implementing these new practices, emphasizing the need for journalists to actively support public life and engage in a mutually beneficial relationship with scholars.

item.title: Newspapers need to give citizens a voice, critics say
item.description: Coverage of a conference about newspapers giving citizens a voice. Jay Rosen is quoted defining public journalism as a self-conscious examination of professional newspaper culture.

item.title: 'Public journalism' gets an ethical going-over
item.description: A panel yesterday discussed the advantages and potential irritants of newspaper writing that begins and ends with an audience in mind - 'public journalism,' termed by The Home News for its innovative reporting approach before an auditorium filled with students at the Busch Campus Center.

item.title: NEGATIVE NEWS misses the point
item.description: By Ross, a journalism professor at New York University and director of the Project on Public Life and the Press, and reporting on negativity, 'We're still missing the entire sale of negativity, not for the sake of negativity, but for the sale of political drama.'

item.title: Journalism
item.description: Article discusses the state of journalism and advocates for a more involved approach. References work by 'Robert Rosen' (likely Jay Rosen) making a case for journalism that is involved as an act of service, in contrast to detachment and uninvolvement.

item.title: Every day a Saturday: Newspapers and community
item.description: Column by Maria Henson about community connections and the role of newspapers in civic life. In the 'Newspapers and community' section, Henson describes attending a conference on public journalism where NYU professor Jay Rosen spoke about journalism that connects communities and fosters public life, and references the 'New Big Village Renaissance' concept.

item.title: What role do you play as citizen?
item.description: A major editorial/opinion piece by Davis Merritt Jr. explaining the public journalism movement as a cultural change in how newspapers relate to their communities. The article includes multiple references to Jay Rosen's work and writings on public journalism, including quotes from his papers for the Kettering Foundation.

item.title: Media advocacy to push causes steps over line
item.description: This article discusses media advocacy and whether it oversteps journalistic boundaries. It cites Roger Tatarian's views on "public journalism" and advocacy journalism.

item.title: Publishers, editors told future lies in 'public journalism'
item.description: Article reports on remarks to Pacific Northwest newspaper publishers and editors about the future of newspapers lying in 'public journalism,' which draws people in and asks them what's worth doing. The article notes declining readership and rising cynicism as motivations for the public journalism movement.

item.title: Journalists urged to try reaching out
item.description: A brief article reporting on a conference where Jay Rosen spoke to Pacific Northwest journalists about public journalism and community engagement. Rosen urged newspapers to use their unique ability to help rebuild community.

item.title: Newspapers must reconnect citizens with issues, execs told
item.description: An article reporting on a conference where newspaper executives in Spokane were encouraged to find innovative ways to reconnect citizens with community issues. The article discusses the Public Life Project, which is related to Jay Rosen's work in public journalism.

item.title: What is R/UDAT? And what am I doing with it?
item.description: First-person article by a journalist describing involvement in an R/UDAT community assessment. The author discusses the rise of 'public journalism' and how journalists can get involved in community problem-solving, mentioning a group at New York University's journalism program.

item.title: Journalists should champion free speech, not fee speech
item.description: A media column criticizing TV journalists like David Brinkley for accepting paid speaking fees, arguing this undermines public trust in journalism. The article references New York University journalism professor Jay Rosen's prediction that journalists accepting paid speaking fees will erode public confidence, and discusses an article in The New Yorker that named and criticized many prominent journalists for this practice.

item.title: Public access, not excess, is media problem
item.description: Richard Harwood's column about the media's problems with public access and engagement. The article extensively references Jay Rosen's work, describing him as a 'New York University journalism professor' who writes about 'citizenship' and the connections between the decline of citizenship and the decline of journalism. Harwood discusses Rosen's observations about the 'culture of entertainment' that competes with newspapers.

item.title: Elite Press Reporting On Elite Government
item.description: An opinion piece by Washington Post media critic Richard Harwood discussing changes in the journalism landscape and the relationship between elite press and elite government. The article references Jay Rosen's writing about how newspaper journalists have been replaced at networks and magazines.

item.title: Mixed message
item.description: A letter to the editor criticizing a statement by Jay Rosen about objectivity in journalism. The letter writer takes issue with Rosen's claim that objectivity should be used to frame problems to enable societal discussion, arguing this suggests journalists manipulate how stories are presented.

item.title: Open phones; A new role for journalism
item.description: An early On The Media broadcast featuring a panel discussion on new roles for journalism. Rosen appears alongside John Dinges and Davis Merritt Jr. -- a key figure in the public journalism movement -- to discuss how journalism might evolve to better serve democratic life. This is one of Rosen's earliest known broadcast appearances, predating PressThink and his major written works.

item.title: A reluctant editor takes the plunge into participation
item.description: An editor describes his changing views on the role of journalists in the community, moving from a traditional objective stance to more active participation in civic affairs.

item.title: President meets the press
item.description: Editorial discussing the relationship between President Clinton and the White House press corps, arguing for more civility and sense. The piece mentions Jay Rosen as being correct in chastising the press corps to exercise more sense and civility.

item.title: Journalism professor barks at press, but the culprit escapes
item.description: An editorial commentary piece discussing a journalism professor's criticism of the press, comparing journalists to barking dogs. The article references journalism professors' critiques of media coverage but doesn't explicitly name Jay Rosen.

item.title: I Am Not Optimistic But I Do Have Hope: The Future of Journalism in A Media Age
item.description: This 1993 lecture distinguishes between 'journalism' and 'The Media,' arguing that journalism's purpose is to foster a public, not merely an audience. Rosen critiques the prevailing view of news as merely 'part of our world' and challenges the notion of journalistic objectivity as espoused by Leonard Downie Jr. He contrasts two visions of American democracy—Hamilton's emphasis on private gain and Jefferson's focus on public participation—and asserts that journalism should align with the latter, advocating for a reinvention of journalism to prevent its absorption into the media industry.

item.title: Study of network TV is out of touch
item.description: Review of a television documentary examining American network television. The review discusses the film's use of ideological analysis of TV, referencing media critics including Peter Ford of the University of California, Berkeley, who argues that TV 'can show you the world' but also that it presents a distorted view. The article references critical perspectives on television consistent with the media criticism tradition associated with Jay Rosen and his NYU colleagues.

item.title: Closing days: Bash the media
item.description: A syndicated column by Hal Rhodes discussing the media-bashing trend during the closing days of the 1992 presidential election campaign. The article discusses how politicians attack the news media as a campaign strategy. In the context of media criticism and political reporting, the article references journalism professor Jay Rosen's work on the relationship between the press and democratic politics.

item.title: Should newspapers print the time of a candidate's TV ad?
item.description: An article by Boston Globe ombudsman Gordon McKibben examining whether newspapers should cover political TV advertising more critically, including printing the time and content of candidate TV ads for voters. The article references Jay Rosen as a 'professor of journalism at New York University' and expert on the intersection of advertising and politics in the context of the 1992 presidential campaign.

item.title: Dems hope to shine with glitzy convention
item.description: Front-page article about the upcoming 1992 Democratic National Convention at Madison Square Garden, examining whether the party could produce a compelling television event. The article quotes NYU journalism professor Jay Rosen on voters' desire for substance over political spectacle, noting the challenge of making the convention feel genuine and engaging to a cynical public.

item.title: Who should the newspaper be published for?
item.description: Article discusses the purpose of newspapers and references Jay Rosen's essay about media trends. Rosen's analysis of the tension between grabbing attention versus serving the community is quoted.
